ARTICLE
Self sovereign identity in e-governance: blockchain
solutions for ﬁntech compliance and citizen-centric
ﬁnancial services
Arjun J Nair 1, Sridhar Manohar 1 & Satish Rao A B 2 ✉
With the growing technology, population and public services, there is a need for ef ﬁcient
transactions with safety and security in e-governance applications. This study proposes a
blockchain supported e-governance digital identity management framework incorporated
with gig-economy strategy and service innovation tools that could enhance the existing
e-governance process. The proposed conceptual model is validated through expert interviews
and fuzzy logic. The process is comprehensive and involves applying the opinions of experts,
as well as con ﬁrming the rules used for the fuzzy inference system through a questionnaire to
obtain a more profound understanding of opinions. The result of the fuzzy logic algorithm
indicates that to ensure the individuals ’ identity is safe and secure, the e-governance appli-
cations must integrate blockchain technology, and to make identity management more
efﬁcient, there needs to augmentation of service innovation and the gig-economy model.
Based on the result of this study, the academicians need to focus on new theoretical and
conceptual frameworks in enhancing the usage of blockchain technology integrated with the
latest technologies such as AI, ML and Metaverse. The government needs to understand that
bringing innovative service models and incorporating the gig economy could help in deter-
mining secure and cost-effective transactions, and can be used for framing the models in
other industries. The proposed model yielded the highest ef ﬁciency scores and better results
compared to the existing models in the literature in terms of enhanced productivity and
performance. Compared to other studies, this study emphasizes the importance of managing
resources through the gig economy, and frequent innovations with secured blockchain would
result in enhanced transactions.

Introduction
T
echnology transformation is fast occurring globally across
sectors, leading to a competitive business environment.
Every industry, irrespective of the type of business, has an
objective to be an early mover, and hence, they diversify their
business strategies. On the other hand, customers expectations
and requirements are marching towards personalized comfort
without compromises. Every manager aspires to sustain for a
longer period. In that case, to sustain itself as a market leader
among competing organizations, it has to focus on innovation in
technological and non-technological aspects, and hence there
evolved co-creation among researchers, academicians, and prac-
titioners evolved. However, this is not the situation with gov-
ernment organizations and agencies, as their motive is to provide
public welfare schemes to the masses at a lower cost.
Most governments worldwide have successfully implemented
their public welfare schemes using Information and Commu-
nication Technologies (ICT) termed E-Governance (Ojo, 2014;
Basu et al., 2023a). The success of providing services such as
healthcare, education, social justice, food safety and security, ﬁrst
aid and prevention of disease, policies and legal support etc. in
developed countries has motivated the governments in develop-
ing countries to provide similar services and enhance their quality
for their citizens. According to Dawes ( 2008) and Business Jar-
gons, (2019), E-Governance is a bureaucratic process of providing
simple, moral, accountable, responsive, and transparent govern-
ance to the citizens, businesses, and others that helps in the
reduction of corruption and at the same time provides services to
the masses. Further, the politicians and government employees
inﬂuence can be reduced through online transactions and com-
fortable with record keeping. For citizens, the technology allows
them to access the service at their convenience, provide deeper
knowledge, access from any location, and multitask without
affecting the quality at less cost, resource, and manpower (Kumar
et al., 2021; Raza, 2024; Nair et al., 2023). E-governance appli-
cation also helps the government in managing the economic
activities at macro and micro-level environments, from ﬁscal to
monetary policies, social upliftment, increase in individual per
capita income, lifestyle, environment and wildlife management.
Speciﬁcally, it helps in the reduction of costs and exclusively
provides personalized services (Dasgupta, 2021; Basu et al.,
2023b).
However, the usage of electronic communication technologies
such as the internet and other digital tools for enhancing the
effectiveness and ef ﬁciency of government operations and public
services has several gaps to be addressed, especially concerns like
privacy and security when it comes to individuals ’ digital identity
management (Basu, 2004; Wang, 2024). One of the key draw-
backs of technology, especially in developing nations, is the digital
divide, the availability of technological devices or knowledge to
very few people and not others. This creates a situation where
only a certain set of the population can access the services online,
thereby causing a hindrance to others from participating in
democratic processes. Further, the usage of technology in gov-
ernance could also increase the risk of cyberattacks and data
breaches, for which governments must be cautious in the security
and protection of sensitive information. One additional require-
ment is the digital literacy of the citizens. Appropriate knowledge
to access and use the government-launched services. Lack of
knowledge and compatibility leads to the exclusion from the
e-governance bene ﬁts, especially those for the unforti ﬁed groups
like the elderly, low-income and people in poverty (Bwalya,
2009). For example, in developing countries like India, where the
population is a major concern, not having an appropriate, ade-
quate infrastructure is also a serious concern. To create and
ensure trust among the citizens, the government has to be
accountable and incorporate suitable infrastructure like providing
high-speed internet, advanced hardware and software, electricity,
and be updated with the latest technology and provide awareness
continuously.
There are numerous technologies and software introduced and
managed to address the day-to-day requirements. However,
academics and researchers favored certain technologies compared
to others by conducting deeper research and industrial sugges-
tions (Wang and Chen, 2024). For example, very few literature
works discuss blockchain technology (a decentralized transaction
database mechanism since its emergence in 2008) compared to
artiﬁcial intelligence, machine learning, metaverse etc. Blockchain
technology was originally invented to support the decentralized
ﬁnancial transaction known as cryptocurrency named Bitcoin;
however later it has been adopted for various other applications
(Alla et al., 2018; Rana et al., 2022; Nair et al., 2023). Three
generations of blockchain technology have been identi ﬁed by
Efanov and Roschin, (2017) as namely: (1) digital currency, (2)
digital economy and (3) digital society. The ﬁrst generation is the
digital currency, which is the platform of underlying protocols
and digital contracts. The second generation is the digital econ-
omy, whereby a variety of economic and ﬁnancial payments,
transfers and transactions occur, such as loans, mortgages, stocks,
bonds, derivatives, as well as legal instruments (Nuryyev et al.,
2021). It also includes an additional feature of computer-assisted
smart contracts, where the related parties to the contracts can
automatically make transparent payments as per the contract
without any manual form ﬁlings. The latest generation is the
digital society which refers to the wide use of applications beyond
money, currency, commerce, ﬁnancial instruments, or any other
economic activity instead it includes art, health, science, educa-
tion, governance and other aspects of communication and culture
(Swan, 2015; Kaur et al., 2022; Manohar et al., 2023; Wang, 2023).
Blockchain has a tremendous success record concerning the
applicability of digital identity database management. Digital
Identity Management (DIM) is the process of managing and
maintaining the individuals ’ complete information recorded/col-
lected from various sources, further processing, storing and
retrieval for future usage securely and safely in digital form
(Samir, 2021).
Though blockchain technology is looked at for its bene ﬁts,
there are also some negative sides. The major drawbacks are
implementation at a higher level, interoperability, alignment with
other technologies and scalability. Several recent studies (Liu
et al., 2023; Yusuf et al., 2023; Sikder, 2023) have also emphasized
that there is a need for a secure platform for digital governance to
deliver public services, as government agencies and departments
would be sharing and using sensitive data. Taking this as a
motive, this study examines options in integrating innovations
and gig-economy practices in existing blockchain-enabled digital
identity management. The paper proposes that adopting/incor-
porating would enhance the trust among the customers. This
study proposes an enhanced Blockchain supported e-governance
digital identity management framework (DIMF) that helps ensure
the con ﬁdentiality of individual information. Further, the study
also helps to understand how Gig-Economy Implementation and
Service Innovation Models could increase the productivity and
efﬁciency of existing e-governance processes.
Review of literature and conceptual connections
Overview. The literature review for this study focuses on key-
words such as blockchain technology, e-governance, digital
identity management, privacy concern and technology transfor-
mation based on content analysis proposed by Ding, (2019). The

related to blockchain technology has increased and there are
numerous reasons related to it like (1) There is an increase in the
requirement of data security in e-governance, (2) advantages
provided by blockchain technology related to transparency and
safety and (3) convenience for governance companies/institution
in providing services to masses accurately. It is also to be noted
that there is no signi ﬁcant contribution in existing literature
connecting blockchain technology and its bene ﬁts for
e-governance and digital identity management. Further, studies
have not shown the signi ﬁcance of the gig economy and service
innovation models in increasing the ef ﬁciency and security of
e-governance applications.
Publication trends among the countries revealed that with 44
documents, the United States ranked as the country with the
highest number of documents published and citations of 1805,
followed by China (37 documents, 929 citations), India (31
documents, 584 citations) and the United Kingdom (29
documents, 654 citations) respectively. Year-wise publication
trend was covered from 2017 to 2023 as the technology was
addressed and discussed, incorporating its bene ﬁts for
e-commerce lately, after other sectors. Keyword co-occurrence
exhibits the list of keywords that were highly occurring across the
literature from seminal papers to current publications. The
keyword analysis helps in understanding the conceptual connec-
tions earlier studies and new connections that can be proposed
for the future. This also signi ﬁes that the emphasis was not much
given by existing literature on incorporating blockchain technol-
ogy, service innovation models and the gig economy in the DIMF
in e-governance.

tamper-proof system that provides a high level of security and trust
(Yang et al., 2020). All transactions are public, allowing anyone to
see the data. This creates a high level of transparency, which can
increase trust in the system and prevent fraud. Blockchain uses
advanced cryptographic techniques to ensure that transactions are
secure and tamper-proof. It relies on a consensus mechanism to
ensure that all nodes on the network agree on the current state of
the ledger (Viriyasitavat and Hoonsopon, 2019)
Smart contracts are self-executing contracts with the terms of
the agreement directly written into code, allowing for the
automation of complex processes and new forms of decentralized
applications (Koulu, 2016). Blockchain technology can integrate
with other technologies and platforms, making it easier to develop
new applications and services and integrate them into existing
infrastructures (Sharma and Sharma, 2022). Blockchain can
automate processes and reduce the need for intermediaries,
leading to increased ef ﬁciency and cost savings. Some blockchains
can handle many transactions per second, making them suitable
for enterprise-level applications. Blockchains can tokenize assets,
such as stocks, bonds and real estate, allowing them to be traded
in a decentralized and secure manner (Benedetti and Rodríguez,
2023).

The above Fig. 3 depicts the technology behind blockchain and
how blockchain technology is used by various bands in both the
private and public sectors. There are three types of blockchain (a)
Public Blockchain, (b) Consortium Blockchain and (c) Private
Blockchain (Yeasmin and Baig, 2019). A public blockchain is a
decentralized network that is open to everyone. Any user can
read, write and participate in the blockchain network. It is
secured through complex cryptographic algorithms that ensure
the integrity of the data stored on the blockchain. A consortium
blockchain is a permissioned network that is operated by a group
of organizations that work together to maintain and secure the
blockchain. It is used for speci ﬁc business purposes and is open
only to the members of the consortium. A private blockchain is a
permissioned network that is operated by a single organization or
entity. It is used for internal business purposes and is not open to
the public. The network participants are controlled and
authorized by the organization or entity.
The major limitations of blockchain, as elaborated by (Yli-Huumo
et al., 2016; Dai et al., 2017;W a d h w a ,2022), are that ﬁrstly,
blockchains are limited in their scal ability, and this is particularly
important for digital identity m anagement. As more people use
digital identities, the number of transactions that need to be
processed will increase, which can lead to slower processing times
and higher fees. Secondly, blockchains offer a high level of security;
they can also be seen as a public ledger, which can create privacy
concerns. This is particularly important for digital identity manage-
ment, where the information stored on the blockchain needs to be
kept conﬁdential (Naik and Jenkins, 2020). Thirdly, there are many
different blockchains available, and they do not always work well
together. This can create challenges for digital identity management,
where interoperability is critical to ensure that identities can be used
across different platforms and services (Bertino et al.,2009; Trivedi,
2023). Fourthly, blockchain technology can be complex and difﬁcult
to understand for non-technical users. This can create challenges for
digital identity management, where users need to be able to easily
manage their identities without needing a deep understanding of the
underlying technology (Manski,2020). Finally, there is still a lack of
clear legal frameworks for blockchain technology in many countries.
This can create challenges for digital identity management, where
legal issues such as liability and dispute resolution need to be
addressed (Smedinghoff,2012).

Digital identity management framework and e-governance .
The DIMF is the collection of information, policies, systems and
frameworks of an individual or an organization, helping in the
identiﬁcation process and differentiating from others online. It
helps in the context of veri ﬁcation, approvals, transactions and
authentications, and hence the tool has to be highly secure and
unique, and the probability of error must be minimal. The key
components of the DIMF are (a) identity creation like individual
detail capturing, (b) Identity veri ﬁcation like biometric authen-
tication/government issued, (c) Identity authentication like a
password or smart cards, (d) Identity management through
centralized system and (e) Identity usage across multiple systems
(Naik and Jenkins, 2020). Digital identity systems are used and
highly appreciated by organizations and businesses to track
employee details, B2B business information, customer relation-
ship management, patient data handling, student record main-
tenance etc (Wang, 2023). However, it is easy to handle, rectify,
manage and process the DIMF for business organizations and
service sectors as the quantity of data is lesser and the quality of
information is high and complete compared to the government
organizations/agencies (Fig. 4). There need for a highly protec-
tive, secure, ef ﬁcient and enhanced E-Governance digital identity
framework with the latest tools and technologies (Dawes, 2008).
Figure 5 below depicts the existing identity management IOT
using blockchain and smart contracts.
The implementation of the latest technology and manage-
ment tools, along with blockchain technology (Fig. 6)i san e e d
of the hour to enhance DIMF for smooth communication
between the administration and the citizens. This offers and
allows every individual in the respective county to access the
public services freely with transparency (Dawes, 2008). Employ-
ing DIMF to supervise resources and administer policies, results
in a citizen-directed system (Palvia and Sharma, 2007).
E-governance provides unshrinking access to government
services and information around the clock every day to users,
and hence governments need to restructure their operations to
improve their service delivery to the point where it is ef ﬁcient,
safe, and secure. In addition, public participation in decision-
making helps the government to achieve the implementation of
its services to the next level (Bannister and Connoiiy, 2019).
Data protection becomes vital and challenging when public
services are provided online. Hence, it becomes necessary to
develop both systems and models that provide and improve the
security of e-government. Speed, services at a low cost, transparency
and accountability are the advantages, whereas huge infrastructure
investments, a loss of interpersonal communication, illiteracy and
cybercrime are the challenges faced by e-governance.

The issues were articulated by integrating the frameworks
depicted in Fig. 4. This integration yields a conceptual model,
which is then subjected to further validation through expert
interviews and fuzzy logic. The validation process is

of the Gaussian functions are established based on the data and

the problem domain acquired from the questionnaire. Next, the
output variable ‘Secure and Ef ﬁcient Transactions is de ﬁned,
along with its corresponding membership function, which is
triangular in this case (Yadav et al., 2021). The parameters of the
triangular function, such as the left and right slopes and the peak,
are set according to the desired output. After de ﬁning the input
and output membership functions, the next step involves estab-
lishing the fuzzy rules that represent the mapping between the
input and output variables. The fuzzy rules can be de ﬁned using
linguistic terms like “if Blockchain is high and the gig economy is
high and Service model innovation is high, then Secure and Ef ﬁ-
cient Transactions is very high ” (Babkin, 2018). The number and
complexity of the fuzzy rules will depend on the problem domain.
Once the input and output membership functions, along with the
fuzzy rules, are established, the fuzzy inference system can be
employed to evaluate the proposed model (Wang et al., 2022).
The system maps crisp input values to fuzzy values using the
membership functions, applies fuzzy rules to determine the
degree of membership of the output variable and then defuzzi ﬁes
the output variable to obtain a crisp value (Bai and Wang, 2006).
To evaluate the performance of the model, the predicted values
are compared with the actual values using metrics such as mean
squared error and with the author ’s predicted values. As the
performance was deemed satisfactory, no modi ﬁcation to the
input and output membership functions or the fuzzy rules was
necessary, as the desired level of performance was achieved.
Enhancing secure and ef ﬁcient transactions: integrating
blockchain, service innovation business model & gig-economy .
The proposed blockchain-based e-government framework is
illustrated in Fig. 7 below, which integrated the concepts of the
gig economy and service innovation models to enhance the
effective, ef ﬁcient and secure transactions in the e-governance
context. The ﬁgure indicates the importance of an interaction that
needs to take place between government departments, organiza-
tions and individual citizens, allowing a peer-to-peer (p2p)
exchange (broadcast) and validation of data being submitted by
individuals. The information sharing between citizens and the
government, such as ﬁlling out forms for tax, marriage certi ﬁ-
cates, business permits, birth certi ﬁcates, visas or passports, is the
process of identity creation, veri ﬁcation, authentication and
validation (Elisa et al., 2018).
The gig economy is the conceptual framework in the manage-
ment domain that explains the trend of hiring and managing
contractors and freelancers on an adjunct/part-time/hourly basis
for short-term projects, managing the irregular capacity in
services. It can play several bene ﬁcial roles in e-governance,
especially in digital identity management. Identi ﬁcation of
specialized talent that is cost-ef ﬁcient with the increasing use of
technology and digitalization. The gig economy can help the
government tap into a pool of highly skilled independent
contractors with expertise in certain areas (Graham et al.,
2017). Can assist government agencies in providing services
more efﬁciently, especially in public transport or parking services.
Citizens can also participate in government jobs on a timely basis
to improve the service infrastructure. On integrating with
blockchain technology, the gig-economy framework would
enhance cost-ef ﬁcient service outcomes (Patwa et al, 2021).
Service innovation is the process of creating new or improved
services to meet the changing needs and requirements of the
market and customers. In emerging economies, there are multiple
gaps, problems, and opportunities to be addressed on a day-to-
day basis to improve the comfort, lifestyle and requirements of

blockchain-enabled e-governance applications.

Scale and formula calculation and results
To calculate the impact of service model innovation for secure and
efﬁcient transactions in e-governance the following steps were
adopted. Step 1: Identify the key metrics that de ﬁne service model
innovation, secure transactions and ef ﬁcient transactions in
e-governance. These could include factors such as:
Service Innovation: Number of new services introduced, user
satisfaction with the new services, reduction in processing time
for services, increase in accessibility and convenience of
services.
Secure Transactions: Number of successful transactions,
number of fraudulent transactions detected and prevented,
level of user con ﬁdence in the security of the system, level of
compliance with data privacy and security regulations.
Efﬁcient Transactions: Average processing time per transaction,
percentage of transactions completed without errors, reduction
in administrative costs, reduction in time required to resolve
disputes.
Step 2: Assign weights to each of these metrics based on their
relative importance. For example, the number of successful
transactions may be more important than user satisfaction with
new services, so it could be assigned a higher weight.
Step 3: Calculate the impact score for each metric by
multiplying its weight by the change in value observed after
implementing the service model innovation. For example, if the
average processing time per transaction was reduced by 30% and
this metric had a weight of 0.3, the impact score for this metric
would be 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09.
Step 4: Sum up the impact scores for all metrics to obtain a
total impact score for the service model innovation. This score
can be used to compare the effectiveness of different innovations
or to track the impact of the same innovation over time.
To derive a scale for measurement, assign numerical values to
the impact scores based on their magnitude. For example, the
following scale:
Low Impact: 0 –0.3
Moderate Impact: 0.4 –0.7
High Impact: 0.8 –1.0
Using this scale, categorization can be done to determine the
impact of different service model innovations and compare their
effectiveness.

deﬁne the impact of the gig economy on e-governance.
These could include factors such as:
● Number of gig workers engaged
● Reduction in administrative costs

with the integration of frameworks and the development of a
conceptual model, the process emphasizes simplifying scenario
design and increasing the success rate in e-governance transac-

the resulting conceptual model to validation through expert
interviews and fuzzy logic, the study ensures a foundation for
subsequent analysis and implementation. Through the applica-

variables, respectively and the establishment of fuzzy rules based

model. The simulation and validation process, facilitated by

components of the service model innovation, the gig economy,

associated with each component, impact scores are calculated and
categorized to assess their respective contributions to secure and
efﬁcient transactions within e-governance. This methodical
approach enables stakeholders to gauge the effectiveness of
different strategies and prioritize interventions accordingly. The
interpretation of results, particularly demonstrated through the
fuzzy inference system in Fig. 8, underscores the interconnectivity
of inputs, blockchain, the gig economy, and service model
innovation with secure and ef ﬁcient transactions. The Mamdani

outcomes signify a structured and rigorous methodology for
enhancing secure and ef ﬁcient transactions in e-governance,
integrating frameworks, fuzzy logic, and expert validation to

Discussions
As for the government services, there were insuf ﬁcient resources,
high costs of services, growing demand, and security issues. This
prompted a study that delves into the integration of blockchain
technology, gig economy practices, and service innovation models
within e-governance frameworks, aiming to enhance ef ﬁciency,
security and accessibility. The key ﬁndings highlight the potential
of this integration to revolutionize digital identity management
and transaction processing in various e-governance sectors (like
healthcare, safety and security, public welfare schemes etc.). The
result helped in calculating the scaled measurements and supports
the government’s deal, ensuring secure and ef ﬁcient transactions,
ensuring citizen satisfaction. As a consequence of digital cyber-
attacks, the occurrence of fraud cases in ﬁnancial transactions,
preparation of fake documents for government bene ﬁts, it is
difﬁcult for citizens to trust or for the government to establish
conﬁdence among their service receivers. Blockchain would be
the best option to resolve this issue, however, the limitation of the
blockchain explained earlier indicates that the technology cannot
manage the transaction at a larger scale (Yli-Huumo et al., 2016
and Dai et al., 2017). Leveraging blockchain’s decentralized ledger
system, governments can establish secure and transparent DIMFs,
mitigating privacy concerns and ensuring data integrity. Fur-
thermore, the study indirectly addresses the risks associated with
different blockchain functions and their potential impact on data
integrity and property loss. The interoperability issues between
disparate blockchain networks, as noted in the study, can
exacerbate these risks, particularly in scenarios involving the
transfer of sensitive data or assets across chains. In light of these
challenges, the study ’s exploration of blockchain integration
within the broader context of digital identity management
underscores the importance of addressing scalability, privacy, and
interoperability concerns. Acknowledging these issues and pro-
posing practical solutions, such as fuzzy logic-based decision
systems and integrated frameworks, the study contributes to the
ongoing discourse on optimizing blockchain technology for
secure and ef ﬁcient digital identity management within
e-governance ecosystems.
In digital identity management, the study highlights blockchain
technology’s provisions on a decentralized and secure framework,
ensuring the integrity and privacy of citizen ’s digital identities. As
digital identity transactions escalate, the demand for processing,
validation, and storage surges correspondingly. This can strain
existing infrastructure, resulting in slower processing times and
increased operational costs, which aligns with the study ’s

establish tamper-proof identity systems, bolstered by the gig

further enhance accessibility and usability, ensuring citizens can
easily interact with digital identity platforms. Moreover, in
transaction processing, blockchain ’s distributed ledger system
enables transparent and ef ﬁcient transactions, such as payment
processing and license issuance. Furthermore, the study ’s
exploration of gig economy principles underscores the potential
for ﬂexible workforce arrangements to optimize resource alloca-
tion and support transaction tasks, improving the speed and
efﬁciency of service delivery within government agencies, and
mirroring successful implementations in companies like Uber
and Airbnb.
Subsequently, by tapping into a pool of skilled independent
contractors and freelancers, government agencies can address
stafﬁng gaps, improve service accessibility, and foster innovation
in service provision. Additionally, blockchain ensures data
integrity and transparency, providing governments with secure
and immutable records of transactions and public information.
Moreover, service innovation emerges as a critical enabler of
e-governance effectiveness, enabling governments to tailor service
offerings, streamline communication, and enhance policy
responsiveness. The study highlights the imperative for con-
tinuous innovation to address resource scarcity, high service
costs, and burgeoning demand, particularly within government
sectors where ef ﬁciency and accessibility are paramount.
Embracing emerging technologies and management paradigms,
governments can transcend traditional bureaucratic barriers,
fostering greater citizen engagement and satisfaction. Service
innovation models can further enhance data accessibility and
transparency by introducing user-friendly interfaces and com-
munication channels. Adopting agile and user-centric approaches
to service design and delivery, governments can adapt to evolving
citizen needs and preferences, driving continuous improvement
and innovation in public service provision. The fuzzy inference
system, employed in the study, demonstrates the ef ﬁcacy of
integrating blockchain, gig economy, and service innovation
inputs to optimize secure and ef ﬁcient transactions, offering
governments a roadmap for effective implementation. Quantify-
ing the statements and opinions yielded more scalable and
applicable results.
E-government initiatives increasingly rely on advanced digital
infrastructures to deliver public services ef ﬁciently, securely, and
transparently. At the core of this transformation lies blockchain
technology, offering immutable records and decentralized control
that can enhance data privacy and trust in digital governance.
With rising concerns around identity theft and data breaches,
blockchain’s cryptographic protocols ensure enhanced privacy
protection for citizens ’ digital identities. Moreover, the emergence
of digital currencies and cryptocurrencies, including Central Bank
Digital Currencies (CBDCs) (Alonso et al., 2025), further bolsters
e-governance frameworks by enabling secure, transparent, and
traceable ﬁnancial transactions. CBDCs, provide governments
with the ability to maintain monetary sovereignty while facil-
itating real-time payments and reducing transaction costs (Zari ﬁs
and Cheng, 2025; Chua et al., 2025). Collectively, these technol-
ogies offer a future-ready foundation for rede ﬁning trust, trans-
parency, and operational ef ﬁciency in public service ecosystems.
The ﬁndings reveal the signi ﬁcance of this research within the
broader literature on e-governance, digital identity management
and emerging technologies. Previous studies have explored the
individual components of blockchain, the gig economy and ser-
vice innovation, but this research contributes by examining their
synergistic effects within e-governance contexts. Service innova-
tion models introduce digital platforms and mobile applications,
streamlining service delivery processes and enhancing accessi-
bility for citizens. Overall, the integration optimizes e-governance
processes, leading to increased ef ﬁciency, security, and accessi-
bility for citizens and government agencies alike. Unexpected
results may arise in the form of challenges during the integration
process. For example, issues related to data privacy, scalability of
blockchain networks, and adaptation of gig economy practices to
government workﬂows may surface. These results underscore the
complexity of implementing integrated solutions and highlight
the need for comprehensive planning and stakeholder engage-
ment. Addressing limitations in the research is essential for
maintaining credibility. Challenges include the dynamic nature of
technology adoption. Acknowledging these encourages future
researchers to build upon this study ’s ﬁndings and address gaps
in knowledge. Potential follow-up research studies could explore
the long-term impacts of integrating blockchain, gig economy
practices and service innovation models in diverse e-governance
settings. Additionally, investigations into regulatory frameworks,
user acceptance and cybersecurity measures could provide valu-
able insights into optimizing the integration process.

needed for the highest effective transaction of their service to
larger audiences. The study also identi ﬁed the speci ﬁc areas in
each construct, such as service innovation, the gig economy and
blockchain, that needed to be considered to manage digital
identity safely and securely and at the same time provide
enhanced services. Socially, the manuscript contributes to the
government and citizens of developing and underdeveloped
countries to ef ﬁciently use blockchain technology, available
resources, and reverse innovation techniques to optimize and
maximize the outcome. Further, it can be understood and con-
ﬁrmed that blockchain is the key technology that could ensure the
safety and security of the data with high transparency and con-
venience. Thus, the government must pursue the technology
availability and implement it in their streams to better serve their
citizens. The integration of the gig economy and service inno-
vation models presents promising avenues for optimizing gov-
ernment services and resource management. Recruiting
specialized talent and leveraging innovative service delivery
methods, governments can enhance service accessibility, ef ﬁ-
ciency and user satisfaction.

research are multifaceted and contribute to the advancement of
knowledge in several key areas. Firstly, the study provides a
synthesis of theoretical frameworks related to digital identity

integrating concepts from diverse disciplines such as technology,
management and public administration, the research offers a

modern governance systems. Scholars have the opportunity to
explore these insights for crafting robust methodologies aimed at
scrutinizing digital identity management and e-governance across
a spectrum of settings. These settings encompass diverse land-
scapes, including but not limited to varying countries, regions,
and cultural milieus. Additionally, scholars can explore the
socioeconomic dimensions, urban and rural environments, to
ascertain the nuanced impact of digital identity management and

Conclusion
To conclude, the study indicated the integration of digital identity
management, blockchain technology, and e-governance highlights
critical challenges and their potential solutions, offering signi ﬁcant
beneﬁts across academic, practical, and societal realms. Addressing
the inherent scalability and privacy concerns of blockchain tech-
nology, the conversation recognizes the growing demand for pro-
cessing digital identity transactions. However, with the increasing
volume of these transactions come challenges related to validation,
storage, and privacy preservation. While blockchain ’s transparent
nature ensures robust security measures, it also raises concerns
about data privacy and con ﬁdentiality. Consequently, there is a
pressing need to balance the scalability limitations of blockchain
with the imperative of protecting user privacy. The study ’si n t e -
gration of blockchain technology into e-governance systems shows
promise in enhancing digital identity security and trust in trans-
actions. Nonetheless, challenges arise from the interoperability and
integration issues between different blockchain networks. The
proposed integration framework offers a structured approach to
overcome these hurdles, leveraging the gig economy and service
innovation models. This approach optimizes resource allocation,
improves transaction efﬁciency, and enhances service delivery while
promoting transparency and accountability.
Despite the potential bene ﬁts, the complexity of blockchain
technology presents barriers to widespread adoption, particularly
for non-technical users. The lack of clear legal frameworks further
complicates its implementation in government systems. To
address these challenges, user-friendly interfaces and educational
initiatives are essential. Governments can empower citizens to
meaningfully participate in e-governance processes by fostering
digital literacy and simplifying complex concepts. Therefore, the
examination of digital identity management, blockchain technol-
ogy, and e-governance frameworks in the study emphasizes the
need for collaborative efforts to overcome existing challenges and
capitalize on emerging opportunities. Addressing scalability,
privacy, interoperability, and user understanding, stakeholders can
harness blockchain technology ’s transformative potential to
improve service delivery, promote citizen engagement, and foster
inclusive governance practices. The primary aim of this research is
to establish a comprehensive framework for digital identity
management, leveraging blockchain technology to enhance
security and incorporating gig economy concepts and service
innovations for more ef ﬁcient transactions in e-governance. The
study employs fuzzy logic techniques and in-depth interviews with
experts to identify the predominant construct and variables. The
results highlight the importance of blockchain in capturing, vali-
dating, and authenticating the digital identity of citizens. The
decentralized and transparent nature of blockchain ensures data
integrity, emphasizing the need for awareness among service
providers about its bene ﬁts for safety and security. The proposed
framework bene ﬁts governments in both developing and under-
developed countries, enabling resource management through the
gig economy and adapting input variables based on sector
requirements through service innovation. Future research can
explore predictive algorithms in the e-governance context using
this model.
